Beginner.title: What's your name?
Beginner.text: Hello! What's your name? Hi! My name is Ben. What's your name? I'm Anna. Nice to meet you, Ben. Nice to meet you too. Are you new here? Yes, I am. This is my first day at the language school. Oh, welcome! I'm in class B with Ms Green. Really? I'm in class B too! Great. Do you want to sit with me? Yes, please. Thank you. You're welcome. Come on — class starts at nine. Okay. My bag is heavy. Can you help me? Sure. Let's go together.

Beginner.title: Where are you from?
Beginner.text: Where are you from, Leo? I'm from Brazil. I live in São Paulo. Wow! That's far. I'm from Spain. I live in Madrid. Do you like Madrid? Yes, I do. It's a big city. Where do you live now? I live near the park, on Green Street. And you? I live with my sister on Hill Road. It's a quiet street. Is your family in Spain? My parents are in Madrid. My brother lives in London. My parents are in Brazil. I call them every Sunday. That's nice. I'm happy you're here. Me too. Let's have coffee sometime.

Beginner.title: How old are you?
Beginner.text: Sara is twelve years old. Her birthday is on 5 March. Every year her family makes a small party at home. This year her mother bakes a chocolate cake. Her father buys twelve candles. Sara's little brother draws a card with a big red heart. Sara's friends come after school. They sing "Happy Birthday" and give her small gifts. Sara opens a blue book and a yellow scarf. She smiles and says thank you. After the cake, they play a game in the garden. Sara feels happy. She says, "I am twelve today, and this is a great day!"

Beginner.title: This is my family
Beginner.text: This is my family. We live in a small flat in the city. My mother's name is Lena. She is a nurse, and she works in the morning. My father's name is Omar. He is a driver. I have one sister and one brother. My sister is sixteen. Her name is Noor. She likes music. My brother is eight. His name is Amir. He has a toy train. We also have a grandmother. She lives with us. She cooks soup on Sundays. In the evening we sit in the living room. We talk and watch a short film. I love my family very much.

Beginner.title: What do you look like?
Beginner.text: My friend Yuki is easy to see in a crowd. She is tall, and she walks fast. She has long black hair and brown eyes. She wears glasses for reading. Today she has a red jacket and blue jeans. Her shoes are white and clean. Yuki smiles a lot. She has small freckles on her nose. Her brother Ken is different. He is short, and he has curly hair. He does not wear glasses. He has a green backpack. When we meet at the bus stop, I say, "Hi, Yuki! Nice jacket." She laughs and says, "Thanks. Ken chose it with me."

Beginner.title: My favourite things
Beginner.text: I like many things, but I don't like everything. I love pizza with cheese. I don't like fish. It smells strong. I like football on TV, and I like walking in the park. I don't like running when it is hot. My favourite colour is green. My favourite animal is a cat. At home I have two books about cats. On Saturdays I listen to music. I like soft songs. My friend prefers loud music. That's okay — we are different. In the café I always choose orange juice. I don't drink coffee. What about you? What do you like?

Beginner.title: Can you help me?
Beginner.text: Excuse me. Can you help me, please? Of course. What do you need? I can't find the post office. Is it near here? Yes. Go straight, then turn left at the lights. Thank you. Also, can I buy a bottle of water here? Yes. They are on that shelf. Please take one. How much is it? One pound fifty. Okay. Here you are. Thanks. Do you need a bag? No, thank you. Can you open the bottle for me? It's tight. Sure. There. Have a nice day! You too. Goodbye!

Beginner.title: What's in my bag?
Beginner.text: Look inside my bag. There is a blue notebook and a black pen. There is also a small pencil case with three pencils. There are my keys on a silver ring. There is a water bottle — it is half full. There is my phone in a soft case. There are two tickets for the bus. There is a red apple for lunch. There is a little packet of tissues. Oh, and there is my student card. There isn't any money today. I left my wallet at home! Tomorrow I will put it in my bag. Now my bag feels lighter, but I need my wallet.

Beginner.title: My phone number is...
Beginner.text: Can I have your phone number, please? Sure. It's 07 812 445 903. Is that zero-seven… eight-one-two…? Yes. Then four-four-five, nine-zero-three. Got it. And your email? It's rita.khan@mail.com. That's r-i-t-a dot khan at mail dot com. Great. I'll send you the class notes tonight. Perfect. What's your number? Mine is 07 330 219 668. Call me if the bus is late. Okay. Should I write your email too? Yes — sam.lee@school.org. Thanks, Sam. See you tomorrow! See you! Don't lose my number.

Beginner.title: Nice to meet you
Beginner.text: It was lovely to meet you today, Priya. It was lovely to meet you too. Thank you for the tea. You're welcome. Do you know the way home? Yes, I do. The bus stop is near the corner. Good. Say hello to your brother for me. I will. Please say goodbye to your children too. Of course. They liked your funny stories. I'm glad. Well… I should go now. The bus comes soon. Okay. Take care, and see you next week. See you next week. Have a good evening! You too. Bye! Bye! Nice talking with you.

Beginner.title: What time do you wake up?
Beginner.text: I wake up at half past six every weekday. First I sit on my bed for one minute. Then I wash my face and brush my teeth. I put on my school clothes and make my bed. At seven o'clock I eat breakfast with my dad. We have toast and milk. At twenty past seven I put on my shoes and leave the house. The school bus comes at half past seven. On the bus I look out the window. I arrive at school at eight. My morning is busy, but I like it. On Sundays I wake up later — at nine!

Beginner.title: Come into my kitchen
Beginner.text: Come into my kitchen. There is a white fridge next to the window. There is a wooden table in the middle. There are four chairs around the table. On the wall there is a clock. It says ten o'clock. There is a sink near the door. Above the sink there are two shelves. There are cups and plates on the shelves. There is a small plant on the windowsill. On the counter there is a bowl of fruit — apples and bananas. My mother is making tea now. The kettle is hot. Please sit down. Would you like a biscuit?

Beginner.title: Where do you sleep?
Beginner.text: My bedroom is small but tidy. My bed is under the window. There is a blue blanket on the bed. Next to the bed there is a lamp on a little table. My wardrobe is opposite the door. Inside it there are shirts and jeans. On the floor there is a soft rug. My desk is in the corner. There are books on the desk and a chair in front of it. Above the desk there is a poster of a football team. My bag is behind the door. At night I close the curtains. Then the room is dark and quiet, and I sleep well.

Beginner.title: Who does the housework?
Beginner.text: Who does the housework this week? I wash the dishes on Monday and Wednesday. Good. Nina, can you vacuum the living room? Yes. I vacuum on Tuesdays. Tom takes out the rubbish. I do that every evening after dinner. Who waters the plants? I do. I water them on Saturday morning. And I clean the bathroom on Friday. Perfect. What about the laundry? Mum does the laundry. I hang the clothes outside. Thank you, everyone. Many hands make light work! Can we watch a film after we finish? Yes — if the house is clean.

Beginner.title: I'm making lunch
Beginner.text: Where is everyone? What are you doing? I'm making lunch in the kitchen. The soup is cooking. Is Mia helping you? No. Mia is doing her homework in her room. And Sam? Sam is playing with the dog in the garden. Listen — the dog is barking! Ha! What about Grandma? She's watching the news in the living room. Okay. I'm fixing the lamp now. It isn't working. Be careful. Lunch is ready in ten minutes. Great. I'm hungry! Wash your hands before you sit down.

Beginner.title: Do you have a pet?
Beginner.text: We have a pet. His name is Momo, and he is a small brown dog. Momo can run fast in the park. He can sit when I say "Sit!" He can't open the fridge — luckily! Every morning I give him food and fresh water. After school I take him for a walk. He likes balls. He brings the ball back to me. At night Momo sleeps near my bed. He is quiet then. My sister brushes his fur on Sundays. Momo is part of our family. When friends visit, he wags his tail and says hello in his dog way.

Beginner.title: Please close the door
Beginner.text: Please close the door. It's cold outside. Okay. Shall I lock it too? Yes, please lock it. And take off your wet shoes. I'm putting them by the heater. Good. Don't put your bag on the table. Hang it on the hook. Done. Can I open the window in my room? No, please leave it closed for now. Turn on the lamp if it's dark. All right. Where are my socks? Look in the drawer. And please tidy your books before dinner. I will. Anything else? Wash your hands, then come and help set the table. Coming!

Beginner.title: My evening at home
Beginner.text: After work I come home at six. First I change my clothes and wash my hands. Then I help with dinner. We eat at half past six. After dinner I wash the dishes or dry them. At seven I check my messages. Sometimes I call my sister. From eight to nine I watch a short show or read a magazine. On Mondays I water the plants. On Wednesdays I take a bath. At ten I brush my teeth and go to bed. My evenings are quiet. I like quiet evenings. They help me feel ready for the next day.

Beginner.title: Is anyone home?
Beginner.text: Hello? Is anyone home? Hi, Aunt Sue. Yes, I'm here. Mum isn't home yet. Oh. Is your dad there? No. He's still at work. He's driving home now. What about your brother? He's in the garden. He's watering the flowers. Shall I call him? No, that's okay. Please tell Mum I phoned. Of course. Are you coming for dinner on Friday? Yes. I'm bringing cake. Great! There's soup tonight, but Friday is pizza night. Perfect. See you then. Bye, Lara! Bye, Aunt Sue!

Beginner.title: A quiet Sunday
Beginner.text: Sunday is my quiet day. I don't go to school, and I don't hurry. I wake up late and drink tea in my pyjamas. Then I read a comic on the sofa. After lunch I listen to soft music. Sometimes I draw pictures of birds. My mum likes Sundays too. She cooks a slow meal, and we eat together. In the afternoon we walk to the corner shop for bread. We don't buy many things. In the evening I phone my grandma. She tells me a short story. At nine I feel calm and sleepy. A quiet Sunday is my favourite kind of day.

Beginner.title: What's for breakfast?
Beginner.text: What's for breakfast today? We have eggs, bread, and some jam. Is there any milk? Yes, there's some milk in the fridge. Do you want tea or juice? Tea, please. Nina, what do you want? I'd like toast with jam, please. And an apple. Good idea. Tom, any cereal? Yes, please. Is there any yoghurt? Sorry, there isn't any yoghurt today. We can buy some later. Okay. Eggs are fine for me. Breakfast is ready in five minutes. Wash your hands! I'm coming. It smells good already.

Beginner.title: At the supermarket
Beginner.text: Excuse me. Where are the apples, please? They're in the fruit section, next to the bananas. Thanks. I'd like a kilo of apples and some rice. The rice is in aisle four. Do you need a basket? I have one, thanks. How much are the apples? Two pounds a kilo today. Great. Also, do you have fresh bread? Yes. The bakery is near the entrance. It's warm now. Perfect. Where do I pay? At the till near the door. Have a good shop! Thank you. I will.

Beginner.title: How much is this?
Beginner.text: How much is this notebook? It's three pounds fifty. And these pens? The blue pens are one pound each. The black pens are eighty pence. I'll take one notebook and two blue pens. How much is that altogether? Three fifty plus two pounds… that's five pounds fifty. Do you take cards? Yes. Or you can pay with cash. Here's a ten-pound note. Thank you. Your change is four pounds fifty. Great. Can I have a receipt, please? Of course. Here you are. Have a nice day!

Beginner.title: I'd like a sandwich
Beginner.text: Hi! What can I get you? I'd like a cheese sandwich, please. White bread or brown bread? Brown, please. And can I have a tomato in it? Sure. Anything to drink? Can I have a cup of tea? Hot tea or iced tea? Hot tea, please. No sugar. Okay. That's one cheese sandwich on brown with tomato, and a tea. Anything else? That's all, thanks. How long is the wait? About five minutes. Please take a seat by the window. Thank you!

Beginner.title: Do you eat meat?
Beginner.text: Do you eat meat, Omar? Yes, I do. I like chicken and fish. I don't eat much red meat. I don't eat meat. I'm a vegetarian. Okay. What do you eat then? I eat vegetables, beans, eggs, and cheese. I love pasta. Do you like spicy food? A little. Not too spicy. What about you? I love spicy food! My mum's curry is great. Do you cook at home? Sometimes. I can make eggs and rice. Can you cook? Yes. I make a good vegetable soup. Come for dinner next week! I'd love that. Thank you.

Beginner.title: A shopping list
Beginner.text: Hi Dan, Can you go to the shop after work? We need some things for the week. The fridge looks empty! Please buy: - milk (two bottles) - bread - eggs (six) - rice - tomatoes - cheese - tea bags - washing-up liquid If they have fresh chicken, get one small pack. We don't need any biscuits — we still have some at home. Also, is there any fruit left? I think we need apples and two bananas. Thanks a lot! Text me if something is missing from the list. Mia P.S. Take the blue shopping bag by the door. Don't forget your wallet!

Beginner.title: Too spicy for me
Beginner.text: Last night I tried a new restaurant with my cousin. The soup was warm and creamy. I liked it a lot. Then I ordered rice with chicken. The chicken was soft, but the sauce was too spicy for me. My eyes watered! My cousin laughed and gave me a glass of water. His noodles were salty but good. For dessert we shared a sweet cake. It was soft and not too sweet. The tea was weak. Next time I will ask for mild sauce. I still had fun. Food can surprise you — sometimes in a funny way.

Beginner.title: We're having a picnic
Beginner.text: Hi everyone! We're having a picnic in Riverside Park this Saturday. We're meeting at 12:30 near the big oak tree by the river path. I'm bringing sandwiches, juice, and a football. Can you bring something too? - Ana: fruit - Sam: crisps - Yuki: a blanket - Leo: paper plates and cups The weather looks sunny and warm. Bring a hat and sunscreen. Wear comfortable shoes because we may walk after lunch. If it rains, we'll go to my flat instead — same time. My mum says we can use the living room. Please text me by Thursday if you can come. I hope you are free! See you there! Mina

Beginner.title: Is there any milk?
Beginner.text: Is there any milk in the fridge? Let me look… No, there isn't any milk. There's some juice. Is there any bread? Yes, there are two slices. Is that enough? Not really. Are there any eggs? There are three eggs. And there's some cheese. Good. We can make omelettes. Is there any butter? Yes, there's a little butter. What about tomatoes? There aren't any tomatoes. Can you buy some? Sure. Do we need any oil? No, we have oil. Just milk, bread, and tomatoes, please. Okay. Back in twenty minutes!

Beginner.title: Thank you, that was delicious
Beginner.text: Thank you for dinner. That was delicious! I'm glad you liked it. Did you enjoy the soup? Yes, it was wonderful. The bread was fresh too. My grandmother's recipe. Would you like more tea? No, thank you. I'm full. Everything was perfect. You're very kind. It was lovely to cook for you. Next time, please come to my house. I want to thank you properly. That would be nice. Let me get your coat. Thanks again. Good night! Good night. Take care on the way home. I will. Bye!

Beginner.title: Meet my best friend
Beginner.text: My best friend is called Mina. We met in Year Five, and we still talk every day. Mina is kind and funny. She listens when I feel sad, and she never laughs at my mistakes. On Saturdays we ride our bikes to the park. We share snacks and talk about school. Mina likes drawing, and I like football, but that is okay. Good friends do not need the same hobbies. Last week I forgot my lunch. Mina gave me half of her sandwich. I smiled and said thank you. She is the person I trust most. I hope we stay friends for a long time.

Beginner.title: My neighbour next door
Beginner.text: My neighbour next door is Mr Patel. He lives in the flat beside ours. Every morning he waters the plants on his balcony. He waves when he sees me leave for school. Mr Patel is quiet, but he is friendly. Sometimes he brings us fresh bread from the bakery. My mother gives him soup when he is ill. On Sundays his grandchildren visit. They play with a ball in the small garden downstairs. I like living near kind people. The street feels safer when neighbours say hello. Tonight I will knock on his door and return a book he lent me last month.

Beginner.title: Our new teacher
Beginner.text: Our new teacher is Ms Rivera. She started last Monday. She smiles a lot and speaks clearly. In class she writes new words on the board. Then she asks us to say them together. Ms Rivera can play the piano a little. On Fridays she plays a short song before we leave. She listens to our questions and never shouts. Yesterday she helped me with a hard exercise. I feel less nervous now. The other students like her too. After school she stays for ten minutes if someone needs help. I think she is a great teacher, and I want to learn more in her class.

Beginner.title: She works in a shop
Beginner.text: What does your sister do? She works in a clothes shop in town. Does she like the job? Yes. She helps customers choose jackets and shoes. My uncle is a bus driver. He starts early. That sounds hard. My dad is a cook in a small restaurant. Cool! Does he cook at home too? Sometimes. On Sundays he makes pasta for us. My mum works in an office. She uses a computer all day. And you? What do you want to do later? Maybe a teacher. I like explaining things. Nice. People around us do so many different jobs.

Beginner.title: Can I borrow your pen?
Beginner.text: Excuse me, Dan. Can I borrow your pen, please? Sure. Here you are. It's blue. Thanks. Mine has no ink left. Do you need paper too? No, thanks. I have my notebook. Oh — can I also borrow your rubber? Of course. Please give them back after the test. I will. You're a good classmate. No problem. Last week you lent me your charger. That's true! Friends help each other. Exactly. Good luck with question three — it looks hard. You too. Let's check answers together later. Deal. Now hurry — the teacher is coming.

Beginner.title: We play football together
Beginner.text: After school, my friends and I play football together in the park. We meet near the big tree at four o'clock. Ravi brings the ball, and Sara brings water bottles. We make two teams of five. The grass is green, and the air feels cool. Sometimes we laugh when someone falls, but we always help them stand up. After the game we sit on a bench and talk. We talk about music, school, and our weekend plans. Playing together makes me happy. I do not need to win every time. I just like being with my friends under the sky before it gets dark.

Beginner.title: Happy birthday!
Beginner.text: Hi everyone! Please come to my birthday party on Saturday. We are meeting at my flat at three o'clock. Bring a smile — and maybe a small gift if you want, but it is not necessary. We are making pizza and a chocolate cake. After food, we are going to play music and a funny game. My brother is decorating the living room with balloons. Please tell me if you can come. Message me by Thursday. I hope to see you there! Love, Elena P.S. Wear something colourful. We are taking photos!

Beginner.title: I'm sorry I'm late
Beginner.text: I'm sorry I'm late. The bus was slow. That's okay. Don't worry. We just started. Still — I feel bad. You waited for me. No problem. Sit down. Here's the worksheet. Thanks. Was the teacher angry? Not really. She said, "Better late than never." Good. Next time I'll leave home earlier. Smart idea. Do you need my notes from the first five minutes? Yes, please. You're very kind. Friends forgive small things. Let's finish this exercise together. Okay. And thanks again for waiting. You're welcome. Now focus — question one is easy.

Beginner.title: Who is that man?
Beginner.text: Who is that man near the door? Which man? The tall one in the grey coat? Yes. He is talking to Ms Green. Oh, that is Mr Costa. He is the new sports coach. Really? I thought he was a parent. No. He teaches football on Wednesdays. And who is the woman with the red bag? That's Mrs Ali. She works in the school office. Ah, okay. I don't like guessing. Thanks for telling me. No problem. If you are not sure, just ask quietly. Good advice. I will say hello to Mr Costa later. Do that. He is friendly.

Beginner.title: People I see every day
Beginner.text: Every day I see the same people, and that feels nice. In the morning the bus driver says hello. At school my classmates wave in the corridor. The librarian smiles when I return a book. After class I buy fruit from the woman at the corner shop. She always remembers my name. On the way home I pass the postman with his heavy bag. In the evening my family sits at the table. These people are not all my close friends, but they are part of my day. When someone is missing, the street feels different. I am thankful for the people around me.

Beginner.title: Where is the bank?
Beginner.text: Excuse me. Where is the bank, please? The bank? Go straight along this road. Then turn right at the traffic lights. Is it far? No. About five minutes on foot. It's next to the post office. Next to the post office — okay. Can I walk there? Yes. Cross the street carefully at the zebra crossing. Thank you very much. You're welcome. Oh — the bank closes at four today. Four? I should hurry then! Yes. Good luck. Have a nice day! You too. Bye!

Beginner.title: At the bus stop
Beginner.text: Is this the queue for the number 12 bus? Yes. Are you going to the station? Yes. How long do we wait? The bus is coming in ten minutes. Look — the screen says 14:20. Perfect. Do I need exact money? You can pay by card on the bus now. Great. Is it crowded in the afternoon? Sometimes. Sit near the front if you can. Okay. Thanks for your help. No problem. Stand behind the yellow line, please. Will do. Oh — here comes the bus! Have a good trip.

Beginner.title: Is the museum open?
Beginner.text: Hello. Is the museum open today? Yes, it is. We open at ten and close at six. Can I buy a ticket here? Yes. Adults are eight pounds. Students are five. I'm a student. Here is my card. Perfect. One student ticket. Enjoy your visit. Thank you. Are the upstairs rooms open too? The painting rooms are open. The garden is closed because of rain. Okay. Is there a café inside? Yes, near the exit. It closes at half past five. Great. I'll look at the paintings first. Have a lovely time!

Beginner.title: There's a park near here
Beginner.text: There are many useful places near my home. There is a park at the end of my street. Children play there after school. Next to the park there is a small library. I borrow books on Wednesdays. Across the road there is a supermarket. My mum shops there every Friday. There is also a pharmacy beside the bus stop. Behind our building there is a quiet playground. Two minutes away there is a café with good tea. I like my neighbourhood because I can walk everywhere. I do not need a car for simple things. When friends visit, I show them the park first.

Beginner.title: Let's go to the cinema
Beginner.text: Let's go to the cinema this evening. Good idea! What's on? There's a funny film at seven and an action film at half past eight. Shall we see the funny one? I need to laugh. Perfect. Shall we meet at the café first? Yes. At six thirty? Okay. Then we can walk to the cinema together. Do we need to book tickets? I'll check on my phone… Yes, there are seats. I'll book two. Thanks. I'll buy the popcorn. Deal! See you at the café. See you. This will be fun.

Beginner.title: I'm lost!
Beginner.text: Excuse me. I'm lost! Can you help me? Of course. Where do you want to go? The train station. My map isn't working. Don't worry. You're not far. Turn around and walk to the big clock. The clock on the square? Yes. Then turn left. Walk past the bakery. The station is behind it. Past the bakery, then behind it — got it. You'll see the blue signs. Follow them. Thank you so much. I was nervous. It happens to everyone. Have a safe journey! Thanks again. Bye!

Beginner.title: Across from the school
Beginner.text: My school sits between two busy roads. Across from the school there is a sports centre with a swimming pool. Next to the sports centre there is a small bookshop. Behind the school there is a car park for teachers. On the left of the main gate there is a bus stop. On the right there is a flower shop. Opposite the flower shop you can see a café with red chairs outside. The post office is around the corner, only one minute away. When new students arrive, I explain these places. Locations are easier when you use clear words like next to, behind, and across from.

Beginner.title: A day at the market
Beginner.text: Saturday morning is market day in our town. There are many stalls in the square. Some sell fruit and vegetables. Others sell bread, cheese, and flowers. People talk, laugh, and choose carefully. There is music from a small radio near the coffee stall. I go with my grandmother. She buys tomatoes and apples. I buy a warm pastry. The air smells sweet and fresh. At eleven o'clock the market is very busy. By one o'clock many stalls start to close. I like market day because the town feels alive. You can meet neighbours and find good food without a big supermarket.

Beginner.title: How do I get to the station?
Beginner.text: How do I get to the station from here? Easy. First, go straight for two blocks. Two blocks — okay. Then turn left at the big hotel. Walk to the bridge. Do I cross the bridge? Yes. After the bridge, turn right. You'll see the station clock. Is it faster by bus? The bus is quicker, but it only comes every twenty minutes. I'll walk. I have time. Good. It takes about twelve minutes on foot. Thanks for the clear directions! You're welcome. Follow the blue signs if you feel unsure.

Beginner.title: My favourite place in town
Beginner.text: My favourite place in town is the river path. I go there because it is quiet and green. In the morning the water looks silver. Birds sit on the stones, and people walk their dogs. I take a book and sit on a wooden bench. Sometimes I meet my friend Nora. We talk slowly and watch the boats. The path is near my school, so I can visit after class. I love this place because it helps me feel calm. When the city is noisy, I walk to the river. Ten minutes there is better than an hour on my phone.

Beginner.title: What time is it?
Beginner.text: Excuse me. What time is it, please? It's quarter past three. Quarter past three? Oh no. My class starts at half past three. Then you have fifteen minutes. Where is your class? In Building C. Is that far? About five minutes from here. You'll be fine. Thanks. Does your watch say the same time as the clock on the wall? Yes — both say three fifteen. Perfect. I don't want to be late again. Go now, and good luck! Thanks, Kai. See you later! See you at four for coffee.

Beginner.title: What's the date today?
Beginner.text: What's the date today? It's Tuesday, the twelfth of March. The twelfth? I thought it was the eleventh. No. Yesterday was Monday the eleventh. Oh! Then my dentist appointment is tomorrow — the thirteenth. Correct. Do you remember the time? At ten o'clock in the morning. Mark it in your calendar. March has thirty-one days. Thanks. What month comes after March? April. And then May. Spring months are my favourite. Mine too. Let's meet on the twentieth for lunch. Deal. I'll write "Amy — lunch" on my phone.

Beginner.title: It's raining again
Beginner.text: It's raining again this morning. Grey clouds cover the sky, and water hits the windows. People open umbrellas on the street. Cars drive slowly through small floods near the corner. I wear my raincoat and boots. At the bus stop everyone looks wet and cold. My friend texts, "Is it still raining?" I answer, "Yes — bring a jacket!" In the afternoon the rain becomes lighter. A little sun comes out, but the ground stays wet. I like rain sometimes because the air smells clean. Still, I hope tomorrow is dry. We want to play football in the park.

Beginner.title: Wear a warm coat
Beginner.text: Wear a warm coat today. It's freezing outside. This one? Or my thin jacket? The thick coat. And take a scarf and gloves. Do I need a hat too? Yes. The wind is strong this morning. Okay. What about my shoes? Wear your boots. The pavement may be icy. Ugh. I look like a snowman! Better a warm snowman than a sick student. Fine. Should I take an umbrella? Check the sky… No rain now, but put a small one in your bag. Done. Thanks, Mum. Bye! Bye! Text me when you arrive.

Beginner.title: I have a headache
Beginner.text: You look pale. Are you okay? I have a headache, and I feel tired. Do you have a temperature? Maybe. My head feels hot. Sit down. Drink some water. Do you feel sick? A little. My stomach hurts too. Then you should rest. No football today. Can I still do my homework later? Only if you feel better. First, sleep for an hour. Okay. Can you call the school, please? Of course. I'll say you're not well today. Thanks, Dad. Sorry about the match. Health comes first. Get some rest.

Beginner.title: At the pharmacy
Beginner.text: Hello. I'd like something for a sore throat, please. How long have you had it? Two days. It hurts when I swallow. Do you have a cough as well? A little, yes. No fever, though. Okay. These lozenges can help. Take one every four hours. Do I need anything else? Drink warm tea with honey. And rest your voice. How much are the lozenges? Three pounds fifty. Here you are. Thank you for your help. You're welcome. Feel better soon!

Beginner.title: Wash your hands
Beginner.text: Healthy habits are small, but they help every day. Wash your hands before you eat and after you use the bathroom. Brush your teeth in the morning and at night. Drink water when you feel thirsty. Sleep for about eight hours if you can. Go outside for fresh air. Eat fruit and vegetables with your meals. Cover your mouth when you sneeze. Keep tissues in your bag. These actions look simple, but they protect you and other people. My teacher says, "Strong bodies start with clean hands." I try to remember that. When I follow these habits, I feel more energetic at school.

Beginner.title: My left arm hurts
Beginner.text: Where does it hurt? My left arm hurts. Here, near the elbow. Can you move your fingers? Yes, but it feels sore. Did you fall? Yes. I fell off my bike this morning. Okay. I'll check your shoulder too. Does your back hurt? No. Only my arm and a little cut on my knee. I see. We'll clean the cut and put a bandage on it. Do I need an X-ray? Maybe. First, sit still and breathe slowly. Thank you. I'm a bit scared. That's normal. You're doing fine.

Beginner.title: See you next Monday
Beginner.text: Hi Nora, I'm going to be busy next week, but I really want to see you. Are you free next Monday after school? I'm going to finish my project by Sunday, so Monday should be okay. We can meet at the library at four, or we can walk in the park if the weather is nice. Message me tonight. If Monday is bad for you, we can try next Wednesday instead. Looking forward to it! Sam P.S. Don't forget your English book — we can study for twenty minutes first.

Beginner.title: A cold winter morning
Beginner.text: A cold winter morning starts in the dark. Frost covers the cars, and my breath looks white in the air. I put on two pairs of socks and a thick jumper. Outside, the trees have no leaves. The street is quiet because many people stay indoors. At the bus stop I stamp my feet to stay warm. School heating feels wonderful when I arrive. At break we drink hot chocolate and talk about snow. Last year it snowed in January, but this year we only have ice. Winter is hard, but I like the early sunsets and warm soup at night. Seasons change, and spring will come again.

Beginner.title: What's your favourite subject?
Beginner.text: What's your favourite subject? I love science. We do experiments, and I feel curious. Nice! I like English best. Stories are fun, and I enjoy writing. What about maths? Maths is okay, but it's hard for me. Do you like it? Yes. Numbers make sense to me. What about history? History is interesting when we talk about real people. Same. Art is my second favourite. I can't draw well, but I try. Trying is enough! PE is fun too — I like basketball. Let's help each other. You help me with English; I help you with maths. Deal. Study friends are the best.

Beginner.title: I have English on Tuesday
Beginner.text: This is my school timetable for the week. On Monday I have maths at nine and English at eleven. On Tuesday I have science in the morning and art after lunch. Wednesday is busy: history, PE, and music. On Thursday I have English again, then geography. Friday is my favourite day because we have only three lessons, and we finish at one o'clock. Break is every day at half past ten. Lunch is at twelve thirty. I write homework in my planner so I don't forget. When friends ask, "When do you have English?" I say, "Tuesday and Thursday." A clear timetable helps me plan my week.

Beginner.title: Can you open your book?
Beginner.text: Good morning, class. Please sit down. Good morning! Can you open your books to page twenty? Which page, please? Page twenty. Look at exercise one. Now, listen carefully. Repeat after me: "I can learn." I can learn. Good. Work in pairs. Ask your partner three questions. Can we write the answers in our notebooks? Yes. And please raise your hand if you need help. Can you explain number two again? Of course. First read the example. Then try. Time's up. Close your books. Well done today!

Beginner.title: I forgot my homework
Beginner.text: I'm sorry, Ms Brown. I forgot my homework. Did you leave it at home? Yes. I finished it last night, but I left the notebook on the table. I see. Can you bring it tomorrow morning? Yes, first thing. I'm really sorry. That's okay this time. Please set a reminder on your phone. I will. Can I still get a mark if I bring it tomorrow? Yes, but don't make it a habit. Understood. Thank you for understanding. You're welcome. Now join the group work. Okay. And I'll email you a photo of the page tonight. Perfect. That helps.

Beginner.title: Let's study together
Beginner.text: Hi Farah, Let's study together for the English test! Are you free tomorrow after school? We can meet in the library at four. I can bring my notes and vocabulary cards. Can you bring the practice questions from page 40? We should review irregular verbs and then do one listening exercise. If the library is full, we can sit in the café near the gate. Message me if this plan works. Looking forward to it — two brains are better than one! Zayn P.S. Don't forget your charger. My tablet battery dies fast.

Beginner.title: In the school library
Beginner.text: Our school library is quiet and bright. There are tall shelves with story books, science books, and dictionaries. There is a reading corner with soft chairs near the window. You can borrow three books for two weeks. There are also computers for homework research. The librarian helps you find titles and reminds you to whisper. At lunchtime many students come to finish projects. I like the library because I can think clearly there. Last week I found a book about space. I read ten pages every day. When the bell rings, I return to class feeling ready. A good library makes learning easier.

Beginner.title: We have a test tomorrow
Beginner.text: We have a test tomorrow. Are you ready? Not yet. I'm going to revise tonight. Me too. What are you going to study first? Vocabulary. Then grammar. I need to practise past verbs. Good plan. Do you want to quiz each other online at eight? Yes! I'll make ten questions. Can you make ten too? Sure. We need to sleep by ten thirty, though. Agreed. A tired brain forgets everything. True. I'm going to put my phone away after we finish. Smart. See you online at eight — and good luck tomorrow! Good luck! We've got this.

Beginner.title: Break time!
Beginner.text: Break time starts at half past ten. Students leave the classrooms and fill the corridors. Some buy juice at the snack bar. Others kick a ball in the yard. A few sit under the tree and talk about games and music. I usually eat an apple and check my messages. Today my friends are laughing near the fountain. Someone is taking photos. The teachers walk around and smile. Break is short — only fifteen minutes — but it feels important. We relax, then the bell rings again. Everyone runs back to class. After break I feel awake and ready for maths.

Beginner.title: Please speak slowly
Beginner.text: Excuse me. Please speak slowly. I didn't understand. Of course. Can you hear me better now? A little. Can you repeat the last sentence, please? Yes. "Write three sentences about your weekend." Thank you. What does "weekend" mean again? Saturday and Sunday. Okay. And can you write the word on the board? Sure. Here — w-e-e-k-e-n-d. Perfect. One more thing: can you check my first sentence? Let's see… Good start! Change "go" to "went." Ah, past tense. Thanks for your patience. Anytime. Asking questions helps you learn.

Beginner.title: My first day at school
Beginner.text: I still remember my first day at school. I held my mother's hand at the gate. The building looked very big. My teacher smiled and said, "Welcome!" I felt nervous and excited at the same time. In the classroom I sat next to a girl called Hana. She shared her crayons with me. At break I cried a little because I missed home. Then we played with a ball, and I laughed again. In the afternoon we drew pictures of our families. When Mum came, I showed her my drawing. That day felt long, but it was the start of many good days. I learned that new places can become familiar.

Beginner.title: What do you do after school?
Beginner.text: What do you do after school? I usually play football with my brother. Then I do homework. Do you watch TV? Sometimes, but only for thirty minutes. What about you? I usually read comics. On Wednesdays I have guitar class. Cool! Do you practise every day? Almost. On Sundays I visit my grandparents instead. That sounds nice. Do you ever go to the park? Yes, at weekends. We ride bikes when the weather is good. Maybe we can go together next Saturday. I'd like that. Free time is better with friends. Agreed. Let's message on Friday.

Beginner.title: I love football
Beginner.text: I love football. I play every Thursday with my school team, and I watch big matches on TV with my dad. My favourite position is midfield because I can run and pass. When we score, we shout and high-five. Last month our team won three games. I also like swimming, but football is number one. My sister prefers basketball. She says football is too muddy! That's okay — we still cheer for each other. On rainy days I practise juggling the ball in the garage. Sport makes me tired, but it also makes me happy. After training I drink water and stretch. Healthy fun is the best kind of fun.

Beginner.title: Can you play the guitar?
Beginner.text: Can you play the guitar? A little. I can play three songs. Can you? No, I can't. But I can sing. Nice! Can you play the piano? Yes, I can. I practise twice a week. Wow. I can't play the piano at all. That's okay. Can you dance? Ha! I can dance a bit, but I'm not great. Same. What about drums? I can't play drums. They're too loud for my flat! True. Maybe we can make a small band — guitar and piano. Let's try next weekend. Music is more fun together.

Beginner.title: We're watching a film
Beginner.text: What are you doing tonight? We're watching a film at my place. Want to come? Maybe. What kind of film? A comedy. My sister is choosing snacks now. Funny is good. I don't want a scary one. Same. We're starting at eight. Are you coming? Yes! Should I bring anything? Can you bring juice? We have popcorn already. Sure. I'm leaving home at half past seven. Perfect. Text when you're near. Will do. This is going to be fun! See you soon!

Beginner.title: A rainy-day hobby
Beginner.text: On rainy days I stay indoors and enjoy quiet hobbies. I like drawing animals in my sketchbook. Sometimes I build puzzles on the table. My brother prefers video games, but I only play for thirty minutes. Then I read a mystery book under a blanket. When I feel creative, I make cards for my friends. Mum makes hot chocolate, and we listen to soft music. Rain on the window sounds like a drum. I don't mind bad weather because indoor fun can be lovely. If you visit me on a rainy afternoon, bring a book or a game. We can share the sofa and forget the storm outside.

Beginner.title: Come to my party
Beginner.text: Dear friends, Would you like to come to my party on Friday? It starts at six o'clock at my house, 14 Oak Street. We are going to play music, dance, and eat pizza. There will also be a small cake at seven. Please wear comfortable clothes — we may dance in the living room! You can bring a friend if you want. Tell me by Wednesday if you can come. I hope to see you there! Love, Yuki --- Thanks, Yuki! Yes, I'd love to come. Can I bring lemonade and some crisps? Yes, please! That would be perfect. See you Friday at six. Don't be late!

Beginner.title: I collect stickers
Beginner.text: I collect stickers. It started when I was eight. My aunt gave me a book with empty pages, and I filled the first page with animal stickers. Now I have hundreds. Some are shiny. Some are funny. I keep rare ones in a special box. At school my friends trade stickers at break. I look for space stickers and cats. Collecting teaches me to be patient. I don't need to buy everything at once. On Sundays I organise my album by colour. My brother laughs, but he collects football cards, so he understands. Hobbies can look small to other people, but they make me proud. Every sticker has a tiny story.

Beginner.title: Let's go for a walk
Beginner.text: Let's go for a walk. The sun is out! Good idea. Why don't we take the river path? Perfect. Do you want to bring a football too? Maybe later. First let's just walk and talk. Okay. Shall we invite Nora? Why not? I'll message her now… She says yes! Great. Meet at the bridge in twenty minutes? Yes. Wear comfortable shoes. And bring water. It's warmer than yesterday. True. If we get hungry, there's a café near the park. Let's do that after the walk. Deal. Fresh air, here we come!

Beginner.title: Weekend plans
Beginner.text: Hi team, What are your weekend plans? I'm going to visit the science museum on Saturday morning. In the afternoon I'm going to play tennis with my cousin. On Sunday I'm going to stay home and finish my English project, but in the evening I'm free. Does anyone want to watch a film on Sunday at seven? We can meet at my place. Bring snacks if you can. Reply today so I can buy tickets if we choose the cinema instead. Looking forward to a fun weekend! Maya P.S. The weather looks sunny — good for outdoor plans too.

Beginner.title: That was so much fun!
Beginner.text: Yesterday was so much fun! In the morning we rode bikes to the lake. The water looked blue, and ducks swam near the edge. We ate sandwiches on a blanket. In the afternoon we played volleyball with two other families. I fell once, but I laughed. Later we listened to music and danced on the grass. When the sun went down, we took a group photo. On the way home I felt tired and happy. I told Mum, "That was the best Saturday." She smiled and said we can go again next month. Fun days stay in your mind long after they end. I already want another one.

Beginner.title: We're going on a trip
Beginner.text: We're going on a trip to the coast on Friday. Exciting! What do we need to pack? Clothes for two days, toothbrushes, and chargers. Are we going to take the train? Yes. I'm going to buy tickets tonight. Do we need snacks for the journey? Good idea. Can you make a list? Sure — water, fruit, and sandwiches. Perfect. Don't forget your raincoat. The weather changes fast. Okay. What time do we leave? At seven in the morning. Set your alarm! Done. I can't wait!

Beginner.title: Two tickets, please
Beginner.text: Two tickets to Brighton, please. Single or return? Return, please. For today. Okay. The next train leaves at 11:40 from platform 3. How much are they? Twenty-four pounds for both. Can I pay by card? Yes. Please tap here… Thank you. Do I need to print anything? No. Show this QR code on your phone. Great. Is the train direct? Yes, no changes. Have a good trip! Thanks. Where is platform 3? Straight ahead, then left.

Beginner.title: What's in your suitcase?
Beginner.text: Look inside my suitcase. There are two T-shirts and one warm jumper. There are jeans and a pair of shorts. There is a wash bag with a toothbrush, toothpaste, and soap. There are socks and underwear in a small pouch. There is my phone charger and a book for the train. There isn't much space left, so I didn't pack extra shoes — only the trainers I'm wearing. There is also a light raincoat because the forecast shows showers. Mum says travellers need less than they think. I checked twice: passport, tickets, and keys are in my hand luggage. Now the suitcase feels ready, and so do I.

Beginner.title: At the hotel desk
Beginner.text: Hello. I have a reservation under the name Hassan. Good evening. One double room for two nights? Yes. I'd like a quiet room if possible. Of course. You're in room 214 on the second floor. Great. What time is breakfast? From seven to ten in the dining room. Perfect. Do you need my passport? Yes, please. And a card for the deposit. Here you are. Thank you. Here's your key card. The lift is on the left. Thanks. Is there Wi-Fi? Yes. The password is on the card. Enjoy your stay!

Beginner.title: The train leaves at six
Beginner.text: Excuse me. What time does the train leave? The train to Leeds leaves at six fifteen from platform 2. Six fifteen — is that the next one? Yes. After that, the next train is at seven o'clock. How long does the journey take? About fifty minutes. Does it arrive on time usually? Today it looks good. There's no delay on the board. Perfect. Doors close one minute before departure. That's right. Please stand behind the yellow line. Thanks. I'll get a coffee and come straight back. Don't be late — six fifteen comes quickly!

Beginner.title: Can you take a photo?
Beginner.text: Excuse me. Can you take a photo of us, please? Of course! Should I take it in landscape? Yes, please. Can you include the fountain behind us? Move a little to the left… Perfect. Smile! Thank you so much. One more? Sure. Ready… done! Check if it's clear. It's great. You're very kind. No problem. Are you visiting for the weekend? Yes. It's our first time here. Enjoy the city. The old bridge is lovely too. We'll go there next. Thanks again! Have a wonderful day!

Beginner.title: I need a map
Beginner.text: Hello. I need a map of the town centre, please. Here you are. Free maps are on this shelf. Thanks. Where are we now on the map? We're at the tourist office — here, by the red star. How do I get to the castle? Walk straight to the square, then follow the brown signs. Is it far? About fifteen minutes. You can also use the free city app. Does the app work offline? Yes, if you download the map first. Need help with that? I've got it. Thank you for your help! Enjoy exploring!

Beginner.title: Our holiday photos
Beginner.text: Last summer we went to a small town by the sea. I took many holiday photos. In one photo we stand on the pier and wave. In another, Dad buys ice cream, and Mum laughs. We visited a museum about ships and walked on the beach at sunset. One evening we got lost for ten minutes, then found our hotel again. Those photos help me remember the trip. When friends ask, "How was your holiday?" I show them my phone album. The colours look bright, and everyone looks happy. Holidays end, but pictures keep the feeling alive. Next year I want to go back and take even more.

Beginner.title: Is breakfast included?
Beginner.text: Good morning. Is breakfast included? Yes, it is. Breakfast is from seven to ten. Great. Is Wi-Fi included too? Yes. Free Wi-Fi in all rooms. Perfect. Are towels replaced every day? Yes. Leave them on the floor if you want clean ones. Is there a gym? Yes, on the first floor. It's open until nine at night. One more thing — is late checkout possible tomorrow? Until twelve, for a small fee. Shall I add it? Yes, please. Thank you for your help. You're welcome. Enjoy the rest of your stay!

Beginner.title: Home again
Beginner.text: We are home again after five days away. The suitcase is open on the floor, and dirty clothes wait for the washing machine. I feel tired but happy. The trip was short, yet full of new streets, new food, and new photos. Mum makes tea, and Dad checks the post. My bed looks softer than the hotel bed. I unpack slowly and put my souvenirs on the shelf. Tomorrow school starts, but tonight I look at my pictures again. Travel changes you a little. Coming home feels safe and warm. I already miss the sea, and I already love my room. Both feelings can be true at once.

Beginner.title: Yesterday was busy
Beginner.text: Yesterday was busy from morning to night. I woke up early and helped Mum with breakfast. Then I went to school and had a long maths test. At lunch I sat with my friends and laughed about a funny video. After school I had football practice until five. On the way home I bought bread from the bakery. In the evening I finished my homework and washed the dishes. At nine I called my grandmother. She asked about my day, and I told her everything. Finally I brushed my teeth and slept well. Busy days make me tired, but they also make good stories. Today I feel proud of yesterday.

Beginner.title: We celebrated New Year
Beginner.text: We celebrated New Year at home with my family. In the evening we cooked a big meal together. My uncle brought juice, and my aunt baked a cake. We put on warm jumpers and waited for midnight. At eleven we played a board game and told old stories. Then we counted down from ten. When the clock struck twelve, we hugged and said, "Happy New Year!" Outside, we heard music and happy voices. My little cousin fell asleep on the sofa soon after. I watched the fireworks from the window. The colours lit the dark sky. That night felt special because we were all together. I hope next year is kind to us.

Beginner.title: A surprise gift
Beginner.text: Last Friday my sister gave me a surprise gift. I came home from school and found a small box on my desk. Inside there was a blue notebook and a silver pen. A note said, "For your stories — love, Amira." I felt warm and happy. I didn't expect a gift because it wasn't my birthday. Amira smiled from the doorway and said I write every day, so I should have nice tools. We sat on the bed and I wrote the first page about her kindness. Then we shared biscuits and tea. Small gifts can mean a lot. I still use that pen, and every time I do, I remember her smile.

Beginner.title: I lost my keys
Beginner.text: On Monday I lost my keys. First I looked in my bag. They were not there. Then I checked my coat pockets. Still nothing. I felt worried because Mum needed the house key. Next I walked back to school and asked the office. A kind teacher found them near the sports hall. Someone had given them in. I said thank you many times. Then I put the keys on a bright ring so I can see them easily. That evening I told Mum the whole story. She was calm and said, "Problems happen. Solutions come when you look carefully." I learned to slow down and check twice before I leave.

Beginner.title: My first bike
Beginner.text: When I was seven, I got my first bike. It was red and small, with white wheels. Dad held the seat while I tried to ride. At first I fell on the soft grass. I cried, then I tried again. After many afternoons I could ride alone to the end of our street. I felt free and tall. My friends clapped when I stopped without falling. Mum took a photo near the gate. I still have that bike photo on my wall. The bike is too small for me now, but the memory is big. Childhood gifts stay in your heart. Every time I see a red bike, I smile.

Beginner.title: The day it snowed
Beginner.text: I remember the day it snowed last winter. In the morning I looked out the window and saw white roofs. Soft snow was falling on the cars and trees. School closed after lunch because the roads were dangerous. We put on boots and gloves and ran outside. My brother and I built a small snowman with a carrot nose. Then we had a snowball fight until our hands were cold. Mum called us in for hot soup. While we ate, snow was still falling quietly. That evening the town looked magical under the street lights. I wrote about the day in my diary. Weather can make ordinary days unforgettable.

Beginner.title: We won the game!
Beginner.text: Last Saturday our school team won the game! The score was three to two. I played for forty minutes and passed the ball for the second goal. When the final whistle blew, we jumped and hugged. Our coach smiled and said we worked hard as a team. Parents clapped from the side. My best friend scored the winning goal in the last minute. After the match we drank water and took a team photo. On the bus home we sang loudly. I felt proud and a little tired. Winning is nice, but playing together felt even better. That night I slept with my muddy socks still in my bag — I was too happy to care.

Beginner.title: Thank-you message
Beginner.text: Dear Aunt Layla, Thank you for the wonderful weekend at your house. I enjoyed the garden walk, the funny films, and your lemon cake. You were so kind to me. The blue scarf you gave me is already my favourite. I wore it on the train home, and it kept me warm. Mum says thank you too for the jar of honey. Please tell Uncle that his card tricks made us laugh a lot. I hope I can visit again soon. You made a normal Saturday feel special. With love, Samir P.S. I attached a photo from the garden. Smile!

Beginner.title: Looking forward to next week
Beginner.text: Hi everyone, I'm looking forward to next week! On Monday I'm going to start my new art class. On Wednesday we're going to visit the city museum with school. At the weekend I'm going to see my cousins — we'll probably play football in the park if it doesn't rain. I'm a bit nervous about art class, but I will try my best. Message me if you want to meet on Sunday evening. I will bring snacks. This week already feels full of good things. See you soon! Love, Rana P.S. I will send photos from the museum.

Beginner.title: A story I like to tell
Beginner.text: There is a story I like to tell at family dinners. When I was nine, I tried to bake bread alone. I mixed flour and water, but I forgot the yeast. The dough stayed flat and sad. I put it in the oven anyway. Twenty minutes later we had a hard, pale brick. Everyone laughed, and then Grandma showed me the correct steps. The second loaf rose and smelled wonderful. We ate it with butter and honey. I tell this story because it teaches me something simple: mistakes can become funny lessons. Now I bake better bread, and I still laugh at that first brick. Good stories feed us as much as good food.

Elementary.title: What was your first day like?
Elementary.text: My first day at the language school felt longer than a normal week. I arrived twenty minutes early because I was afraid of being late, and I stood outside the glass doors checking my bag again and again. Inside, the hallway smelled of coffee and new paper. A receptionist smiled and gave me a blue card with my classroom number. When I sat down, nobody spoke at first. Then a girl next to me asked where I was from, and suddenly the room became easier. The teacher was younger than I expected. She wrote three questions on the board and said we should answer them with a partner. My partner talked faster than me, but she waited when I searched for words. By lunchtime I had already learned ten new phrases and forgotten half of them. Still, I walked home feeling proud. First days are rarely perfect, but they teach you that courage can be quiet. If you show up, listen, and try, the strange place starts to feel possible. What surprised me most was how ordinary the turning point felt. There was no dramatic music, only a choice that looked small from outside. When I talk about memories & firsts with friends now, I try to include that ordinary moment, because learners need real scenes, not only slogans. Practising the language of first days & nerves makes those scenes easier to share without freezing.

Elementary.title: Have you ever got lost?
Elementary.text: I have got lost more than once, but the worst time was in a city I did not know well. My phone battery died after I left the museum, and the street names looked similar. I walked in a circle for almost half an hour. Every café seemed busier than the last, and I felt too shy to interrupt people who were rushing. Finally I asked an older man outside a bookshop. He listened carefully, then pointed to a tram stop across the road. “You should take line three,” he said. “If you stay on for four stops, you will see the river, and your hotel is near the bridge.” His directions were clearer than the map in my head. On the tram I watched the city pass and practised the street name silently. When I reached the hotel, I charged my phone immediately. I have learned a simple rule since then: before a long walk, check your battery and write one address on paper. Getting lost can become a story later, but in the moment you need a calm plan more than pride. If I could speak to myself at the beginning of that story, I would say: slow down, ask one clear question, and accept that first attempts sound imperfect. “Have you ever got lost?” taught me that progress often looks messy in the middle. I still make mistakes with getting lost words, yet I use them more bravely because the topic matters to my real life.

Elementary.title: When did you first cook alone?
Elementary.text: Last month I cooked dinner alone for the first time. My flatmates were away, and the kitchen suddenly looked larger and quieter than usual. I chose pasta because it seemed safer than meat. I boiled water, added salt, and watched the clock like a nervous student. The sauce was harder than the video made it look. I cut the onions too slowly, and they made my eyes water. Still, the smell in the kitchen became warmer and more inviting. When I tasted the first forkful, it was saltier than I wanted, but it was edible. I sat by the window and ate without my phone. That small choice made the meal feel more important. I have cooked many times with help, but cooking alone taught me something different: mistakes are private, and success belongs only to you. If I cook alone again, I will prepare the ingredients before I turn on the heat. First cooking nights are rarely elegant, yet they matter. They show you that independence can begin with one simple plate. Afterward I wrote three short sentences in my notebook: what happened, why it mattered, and what I would change next time. That tiny habit turned “When did you first cook alone?” into practice, not only reading. What was cooking without help like? The honest answer changes as I collect more examples from memories & firsts, and that change is a sign of learning.

Elementary.title: What was your first big mistake?
Elementary.text: My first big mistake at work was sending the wrong file to a client. I was tired, I clicked too quickly, and I pressed send before I checked the name. Ten minutes later my manager called. Her voice was calm, but I could hear the problem. I apologised immediately and sent the correct document. The client was patient, yet I felt smaller than the chair I sat on. That afternoon I made a checklist on a sticky note: name, date, attachment, final read. It looked childish, but it worked. I have not repeated that mistake since then. Mistakes feel worse the first time because you do not yet know how to repair them. Later you learn that honesty is faster than hiding. If you make a serious error, you should say what happened, fix it, and write one step that prevents it next time. People respect repair more than perfection. My first big mistake still embarrasses me a little, but it also taught me to slow down when my hands move faster than my thoughts. People around me reacted differently—some joked, some listened carefully, one person changed the subject. Their reactions taught me as much as the event itself. Talking about mistakes & lessons needs patience with other people’s comfort levels. I learned to offer my story once, then leave space, which feels more grown-up than forcing agreement.

Elementary.title: Do you remember your first friend?
Elementary.text: I still remember my first real friend from primary school. His name was Leo, and he sat two desks away. On the third day he offered me half his sandwich because I had forgotten mine. It was not a dramatic scene. He simply pushed the sandwich across and said, “You look hungry.” That small action felt bigger than any speech. We started walking home the same way. He talked about football; I talked about comics. Our interests were different, but our laughter matched. When another child laughed at my accent, Leo stood closer and changed the subject. I have had many friends since then, yet first friends stay special because they arrive when you still feel new in the world. Childhood friendships are often simpler than adult ones. You do not negotiate calendars or careers. You share snacks, secrets, and scraped knees. If I met Leo today, I might not recognise his face at once, but I would recognise the feeling: someone chose kindness before they knew my whole story. Looking back, the hardest part was not vocabulary. It was admitting I needed help, time, or a second try. Stories like “Do you remember your first friend?” remind Elementary learners that courage can be quiet. When how do childhood friendships begin appears again, I want my first move to be curiosity, not panic, and my second move to be a simple plan I can actually keep.

Elementary.title: What was the first film that moved you?
Elementary.text: The first film that truly moved me was about two sisters who lived in a small coastal town. I watched it on a rainy Sunday when I was fifteen. I expected a light story, but the quieter scenes hit harder than the loud ones. One sister wanted to leave; the other wanted to stay. Their arguments sounded like real kitchens, not movie speeches. Near the end, nobody made a perfect speech. They simply stood on a wet pier and admitted they were afraid of losing each other. I cried in a way that surprised me. Since then I have watched cleverer films and more famous ones, but few have felt as honest. I think stories move us when they show ordinary courage. If a film only chases big effects, it might entertain you for two hours and leave nothing behind. The films that stay are often slower and closer to daily life. That first emotional film taught me to notice small dialogues. Sometimes the most important line is almost whispered. Later the same week, a small detail from “What was the first film that moved you?” came back while I was doing something ordinary—washing a cup, waiting for a bus, unlocking my door. I realised which story first made you feel deeply is not only a classroom question. It shows up in quiet moments when nobody is testing you. Thinking about films & emotion in simple English helped me name the feeling instead of pushing it away.

Elementary.title: Have you ever felt truly proud?
Elementary.text: Hi Maya, I wanted to tell you about something that made me genuinely proud this week. I have finally finished the short course I started in March. For months I studied after work when I was tired, and some evenings I almost quit. On Thursday I got the final result, and it was better than I expected. The proud feeling was quieter than celebration photos online. I made tea, sat by the window, and read the certificate twice. I thought about all the nights when motivation felt thinner than cold soup. Showing up on those nights mattered more than the easy ones. If you ever start something long and slow, you should protect the small routines that keep you moving. Pride is not only about winning. Sometimes it is about proving to yourself that you can keep a promise. Thanks for encouraging me when I complained. Next time you finish a hard thing, message me so I can cheer for you too. Lina What surprised me most was how ordinary the turning point felt. There was no dramatic music, only a choice that looked small from outside. When I talk about memories & firsts with friends now, I try to include that ordinary moment, because learners need real scenes, not only slogans. Practising the language of pride & achievement makes those scenes easier to share without freezing.

Elementary.title: When did you first travel without family?
Elementary.text: The first time I travelled without my family, I went to a nearby city with two classmates for a weekend. The train felt faster than usual, maybe because nobody was reminding me to keep my ticket safe. At the hostel we shared a room with strangers who snored politely and offered us biscuits at midnight. Independence smelled like cheap shampoo and city rain. We got lost twice, argued about dinner once, and still laughed more than we worried. Decisions were slower without parents, but they also felt more ours. I chose a museum that my mother might not have chosen, and my friends chose a night market that I might have avoided alone. Comparing that trip with family holidays, I noticed less comfort and more discovery. If you travel without family for the first time, you should agree on a meeting point and a budget before you leave the station. Small plans protect freedom. That weekend did not make me an expert traveller, but it showed me I could solve ordinary problems without calling home every hour. If I could speak to myself at the beginning of that story, I would say: slow down, ask one clear question, and accept that first attempts sound imperfect. “When did you first travel without family?” taught me that progress often looks messy in the middle. I still make mistakes with independent travel words, yet I use them more bravely because the topic matters to my real life.

Elementary.title: What was your first interview like?
Elementary.text: How was your first interview? Worse than my nightmares, and also better. I arrived early, then waited in a bright lobby where every clock seemed louder than normal. What did they ask? First they asked about a team project. I explained it clearly, but then my mind went empty on a simple question about weakness. I said I sometimes check my work too many times. It sounded safer than silence. Did you get the job? Not that one. They emailed politely two days later. Still, I learned that interviews are conversations, not exams. You should prepare stories, not only lists. What will you do differently next time? If they ask about failure, I will give a real example and say what I changed afterwards. I have practised with my cousin twice this week. Nervous energy is useful if you aim it at listening, not at panic. Do you still think about it now? Yes, especially when similar situations start. I breathe once, then I choose one clear sentence instead of ten nervous ones. What would you tell a younger learner? Prepare two real examples about interviews & nerves, and practise them aloud. Silence feels safer, but a short honest answer builds more confidence.

Elementary.title: Why do first times stay with us?
Elementary.text: I think first times stay with us because the brain treats newness like bright paint. When everything is unfamiliar, details stick: the smell of a classroom, the weight of a suitcase handle, the exact sentence someone said. Later experiences can be happier or more successful, yet they often feel softer because we already know the pattern. First times also carry risk. You do not yet know the ending, so your attention becomes sharper. That sharp attention writes a stronger memory. I have moved house several times, but I still remember the first night in my own flat more clearly than later ones. The kettle sounded louder. The street outside felt more foreign. If life only repeated safe routines, memory would have fewer landmarks. Firsts give us markers for growing up. Of course not every first is pleasant. Some are awkward or painful. Even those matter, because they teach boundaries and courage. Looking back, I do not collect firsts like trophies. I collect them like map pins that show where my story turned. People around me reacted differently—some joked, some listened carefully, one person changed the subject. Their reactions taught me as much as the event itself. Talking about memory & novelty needs patience with other people’s comfort levels. I learned to offer my story once, then leave space, which feels more grown-up than forcing agreement.

Elementary.title: Who taught you the most?
Elementary.text: The person who taught me the most was not a famous teacher. It was my aunt, who ran a small bakery before sunrise. When I was sixteen I worked with her for one summer. She spoke less than other adults, but every instruction was clear. “Measure twice,” she said. “Taste before you decorate. If the dough feels wrong, trust your hands.” She corrected my mistakes without making me feel useless. That balance is rarer than talent. At school I had learned facts quickly, but she taught patience, timing, and respect for ordinary work. Years later I still hear her voice when I rush. I think the best teachers leave tools in your mind, not only grades on paper. People who shape us often do it through repeated small moments. My aunt never gave long speeches about success. She simply showed up earlier than everyone and finished what she started. If I ever guide someone younger, I want that same quiet standard: high expectations, steady kindness, and work that smells like real life. Looking back, the hardest part was not vocabulary. It was admitting I needed help, time, or a second try. Stories like “Who taught you the most?” remind Elementary learners that courage can be quiet. When which person shaped your learning appears again, I want my first move to be curiosity, not panic, and my second move to be a simple plan I can actually keep.

Elementary.title: What makes a neighbour special?
Elementary.text: Mrs Karim was the neighbour who made our building feel less lonely. She lived across the hall and always noticed when someone was ill or overloaded with bags. One winter evening my lock froze and I could not open the door. She brought a kettle of warm water, waited with me, and then invited me in for soup while the metal softened. A special neighbour is not always your closest friend. Sometimes they simply make daily life safer. Mrs Karim remembered birthdays without posting about them. She watered plants when families travelled. She also told the truth gently when music got too loud after midnight. I think communities need people like that more than they need perfect parties. If you move to a new place, you should learn one neighbour’s name in the first week. That small step can matter later when a problem arrives. I have lived in quieter buildings since then, but few felt as human. Kindness on the same floor is a kind of local weather: you feel it even when you do not discuss it. In the end, I understood the topic more clearly because I connected it to one real week of my life, not only to a page of rules.

Elementary.title: Have you ever had a strict teacher?
Elementary.text: Did you like Mr Hassan? Like is the wrong word. He was the strictest teacher I have ever had. He collected homework at the exact minute and corrected every tiny grammar slip. That sounds awful. At first, yes. But his strictness was fairer than it looked. He also stayed after class if you asked for help. He said students should struggle a little, because struggle makes memory stronger. Do you think soft teachers are better? Soft teachers can be kinder day to day. Strict teachers can prepare you for harder tests. I needed both. If a teacher only frightens people, that is useless. If a teacher expects effort and also explains clearly, that can change you. Would you choose his class again? Yes. I still hear his advice when I write emails: be clear, be exact, and check once more before you send. Was anyone surprised by your choice? My family was. They expected the safer option. I explained my reasons slowly, and they listened better than I feared. So can strict teaching still help students is still useful? Very. It helps me check whether I am acting from fear or from a real plan.

Elementary.title: Who do you call when things go wrong?
Elementary.text: Dear Nora, Thank you for asking how I am after that difficult week. When things go wrong, I usually call my brother first. He does not try to fix every detail immediately. He listens, asks one clear question, then helps me decide the next small step. If the problem is practical, he might come over. If it is emotional, he stays on the phone until my voice becomes steadier. I have also learned that different problems need different people. For work stress I message my old colleague. For health worries I call Mum. Nobody can carry every kind of trouble alone, and nobody should. You should build a short list of trusted people before a crisis arrives. If your week becomes heavy again, you can call me too. I might not have perfect answers, but I can help you sort what is urgent from what can wait. Support is not only advice. Sometimes it is simply not leaving someone alone with noisy thoughts. Take care, Sam If I could speak to myself at the beginning of that story, I would say: slow down, ask one clear question, and accept that first attempts sound imperfect. “Who do you call when things go wrong?” taught me that progress often looks messy in the middle. I still make mistakes with support & help words, yet I use them more bravely because the topic matters to my real life.

Elementary.title: What did your grandparents teach you?
Elementary.text: My grandparents taught me skills that no app has replaced. Grandad showed me how to mend a bicycle chain in the courtyard behind their house. He never hurried. “If you force the tool, you break the tool,” he said. Grandma taught me to write thank-you notes the same day I received a gift. She believed gratitude should travel quickly. Their lessons were practical and moral at the same time. They saved jars, reused bags, and repaired chairs instead of throwing them away. At first I thought this was only about money. Later I understood it was about respect for objects and time. I have lived in a faster world than theirs, yet their habits still guide small decisions. If young people only learn from screens, they might miss the quiet intelligence of older hands. Grandparents are not perfect, of course. Mine argued about the radio volume every evening. But when I need patience, I remember Grandad’s slow tools. When I need manners, I remember Grandma’s envelopes. People who shape us often live in ordinary rooms, not on stages. Afterward I wrote three short sentences in my notebook: what happened, why it mattered, and what I would change next time. That tiny habit turned “What did your grandparents teach you?” into practice, not only reading. What practical wisdom comes from older relatives? The honest answer changes as I collect more examples from people who shape us, and that change is a sign of learning.

Elementary.title: Can a stranger change your day?
Elementary.text: One rainy Tuesday a stranger changed my day in less than three minutes. I was late for an exam and my umbrella broke at the bus stop. Papers in my folder started to curl. A woman beside me noticed, opened her larger umbrella over both of us, and said, “Share this until the bus comes.” She did not ask my name. She simply solved the immediate problem. When the bus arrived, she got off at the next stop and waved once. I never saw her again. That short kindness did not make the exam easier, but it stopped my panic from growing. I walked into the room less wet and less alone. Since then I have tried to notice people who are one small difficulty away from a worse morning. If everyone waits for heroic acts, ordinary days stay harder than they need to be. Strangers cannot replace friends, yet they can interrupt a spiral. I think cities feel safer when people allow tiny moments of care. You might never learn the ending of those stories. That is fine. Not every useful kindness needs a sequel. People around me reacted differently—some joked, some listened carefully, one person changed the subject. Their reactions taught me as much as the event itself. Talking about kindness from strangers needs patience with other people’s comfort levels. I learned to offer my story once, then leave space, which feels more grown-up than forcing agreement.

Elementary.title: Why do some friends feel like family?
Elementary.text: Some friends feel like family because they stay when life becomes inconvenient. They know your unfinished sentences. They remember the anniversary of a hard day without being asked. I have one friend like that. We do not live in the same city now, but our conversations still feel like coming home after a long walk in cold air. Family is given; friendship is chosen. That choice creates a special loyalty. Chosen family often listens without ranking your problems. They can also tell you hard truths more safely than distant relatives sometimes do. Of course friendship needs care. If you only message when you need help, the relationship thins. I think the friends who feel like family share three things: time, honesty, and humour. Time builds history. Honesty builds trust. Humour keeps heavy days from becoming permanent. You should protect those friendships the way people protect important addresses. They are rare, and they make ordinary adulthood less lonely. Looking back, the hardest part was not vocabulary. It was admitting I needed help, time, or a second try. Stories like “Why do some friends feel like family?” remind Elementary learners that courage can be quiet. When what turns friends into chosen family appears again, I want my first move to be curiosity, not panic, and my second move to be a simple plan I can actually keep.

Elementary.title: Who inspires you at work?
Elementary.text: Who inspires you at work these days? Our team lead, Rina. She has handled two difficult projects this year without turning stress into shouting. What does she do differently? She explains priorities clearly. If a task can wait, she says so. If a deadline is real, she protects focus time. I have watched her give credit in meetings instead of collecting it. That sounds rare. It is. Some managers only notice mistakes. She notices improvement too. Last month she asked me to lead a short presentation because she thought I was ready.
